items.title: It’s Time to Rethink How You Read the Bible, Chicago Pastor Says
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "The Word of God is the living seed that actually brings new life."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

With the Christmas season kicking into high gear and a new year around the corner, many Christians are starting to think about spiritual disciplines, about setting goals of reading through the Bible and establishing practical ways to prioritize spending time with God. For some, though, diving into the pages of Scripture can feel intimidating and overwhelming.

Chicago-area Pastor Colin Smith, a native of Edinburgh, Scotland, recently appeared on CBN’s “Faith in Culture,” where he explained the importance of understanding what the Bible is meant to do: not simply inform us, but transform us.

“I try in conversations … to guide people away from thinking that the Bible is essentially information,” he said. “The Word of God is the living seed that actually brings new life.”

Smith, who recently stepped down as senior pastor of The Orchard Evangelical Free Church in Arlington Heights, Illinois, after a 30-year tenure, is the author of three guides to read through Scripture, “Fly Through the Bible,” “Drive Through the Bible,” and “Hike Through the Bible.”

After leaving Edinburgh, Smith moved to London to study theology and then spent 16 years in ministry there, before moving to Chicago. His experience across several cultures, he said, reinforced his belief that, despite human beings’ differences, their deepest need is universal.

“The differences are significant, but they are actually superficial,” he explained. “The wonderful thing to me is that the Word of God speaks directly to every person in every culture, in every generation — and that never changes.”

Smith’s three guides through the Bible — “Fly,” “Drive,” and “Hike” — are associated with his ministry, Open the Bible, and each provides a different entry point into studying Scripture, helping readers understand God’s story of redemption, as Smith says, “from the garden to the city.”

“Fly Through the Bible” gives readers a broad overview through five Old Testament figures, five significant events in Jesus’ earthly life, and five gifts God grants to believers. “Drive Through the Bible” expands that framework into a 30-day devotional and “Hike Through the Bible” takes readers through 50 chapters over the course of one year, a study Smith intended for small groups or personal discipleship.

Part of what can make Scripture reading so burdensome is the feeling of needing to perfectly understand every detail of the text. Smith warned against allowing that to become a barrier to digging into the Bible.

“Read something and look for something that you can take into your mind and heart and carry with you, kinda chew on, meditate on during the day, make your own, and seek to kind of live on it,” said Smith.

Gloo and Barna Group has released data showing weekly Bible reading is trending upward. In 2025, Scripture reading among U.S. adults climbed to 42% — a 12-point increase from a 15-year low of 30% in 2024. And among self-identified Christians, the rate is 50%, the highest level in more than a decade. Interestingly, though, Lifeway Research recently polled more than 2,000 American Christian churchgoers with dozens of questions on general Bible knowledge, about 65% scored below 60%. So, while there has been an uptick in Scripture interest, that has not necessarily correlated to greater awareness.

But Smith wasn’t discouraged, reiterating that believers’ goals shouldn’t be to win trivia contests. Instead, they should see Scripture as a tool for understanding and knowing the character of God, and allowing that to shape their thinking, feelings, and daily lives.

“It’s not simply learning a book; this is the word of God,” he said. “This is how God speaks to you.”

Smith encouraged believers to be willing to step into discomfort in reading Scripture. He pointed to Paul, who wrote in 2 Corinthians 12:10, “For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (ESV). The pastor pointed out that Paul was certainly not weak to begin with, having endured imprisonment, beatings, and three shipwrecks. What the apostle was getting at, Smith explained, was that God often calls us to act in obedience when the tasks He hands us are overwhelming.

“Jesus doesn’t want us to splash around in the shallows,” Smith said. “He wants us to launch out into the deep.”

That has been a central part of Smith’s own life. He recalled a letter he received from a professor and mentor when he was considering becoming a pastor. The professor wrote to Smith: “If you do this you will soon find yourself out of your depth, and you will prove God in ways you never thought possible.”

“I think that’s the story of my life,” Smith reflected.

Listen to our full conversation with Pastor Colin Smith in the “Faith in Culture” podcast above.

items.title: Noah’s Ark Researcher Reveals Stunning New Detail About Wood Discovered at the Site
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

There’s yet another major development surrounding Noah’s Ark. Wood uncovered at a site some believe houses the famed vessel’s remains has officially been dated to 4,300 years ago, though many questions persist.

Andrew Jones, founder of Noah’s Ark Scans, a group managing the dig at the site, told CBN News that researchers collected two plastic bags worth of “burned-looking wood samples.” Researchers sent two samples for testing, with one going through a fast-track process in Florida.

“We got the results back on Nov. 18,” Jones said. “The wood samples from this location on the Durupinar … boat site are dating around 4,300 years old.”

Some biblical chronologies would align with this timing, though the Septuagint would place it earlier. Jones said he’s aware of the debate on timing, but is not concerned about those factors at the moment.

“We’re just reporting the results of what we’ve done so far,” he said. “Now we have two more labs that are going to report the results over the next couple months. One’s a lab in Turkey — a Turkish government facility — and then the other one is a lab in Switzerland.”

These results should give additional information that will help to frame and contextualize the wood findings. Jones said one of the lead researchers also plans to ask a Turkish lab to “help determine the type of species, the type of wood it is, if possible.”

Jones said, though he has been confident about the site, he is taking research and results one step at a time, taking great care to come to science-based conclusions.

“We know there’s a worldwide interest in this project,” Jones said. “And so we said, ‘Hey, this is what the wood showed. … We don’t know what the other two labs will show.'”

He continued, “So we’re just doing step-by-step.”

Some critics have long alleged the boat-shape structure underground is composed of stone and not wood, which has still been undetermined. Regardless, the discovery of wood at the site has been shocking to some who ponder whether the wood could be some sort of evidence for remnants from the biblical flood.

“These lines of evidence pointing to this being not just a natural ship shape there, but the buried decayed remains of the ark — this is another line of evidence that we never had before that was recently discovered and now tested by independent lab,” Jones said. “We have more tests coming up that’s pointing to whatever’s in there dating to the time of the flood.”

He added, “From there, people can debate the Carbon-14 dates from a creationist standpoint. They can debate, if it was post-flood, it got in there somehow.”

Researchers will also explore evidence of potential pitch on the wood or another such coating.

Jones encouraged people to pray for the project.

“We just ask that God give everybody wisdom in navigating these issues, and the scientific method, and making sure if it is really Noah’s Ark,” he said.

items.title: KB Has a Warning for Anyone Paid to Talk About Jesus: Don’t Get ‘Good at Doing God’
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: In hip-hop, there’s a move everyone recognizes. An artist gets arrested or caught in a scandal, and a statement goes out that he’s “been meeting with his pastor.” KB has watched that move for most of his career, and he doesn’t entirely mind it. “I like that people see Jesus as a restorative healer,
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

In hip-hop, there’s a move everyone recognizes. An artist gets arrested or caught in a scandal, and a statement goes out that he’s “been meeting with his pastor.”

KB has watched that move for most of his career, and he doesn’t entirely mind it.

“I like that people see Jesus as a restorative healer, someone that helps to settle us, recover us,” he told RELEVANT. “But there is also this historical kind of legacy of people using Jesus as a mascot for their own agenda.”

That worry runs through his sixth album, THIS CANNOT BE SOLD. KB, born Kevin Burgess, started writing it at a moment when, he said, “it felt like the gospel was so for sale that it was to your advantage to package what you are doing as either adjacent to Christianity or directly from the heart of Jesus.”

“That’s a historical anomaly,” he said. “By and large, Jesus has historically been a disruptor, one that doesn’t fit well with our marketing campaigns.”

He borrows a phrase from Dallas Willard for what he was writing against.

“It’s a kind of vampire Christianity that wants Jesus for his blood, but they do not want him for his life,” KB said. “And I felt this strong conviction when I was writing this record that if we are not people that want Jesus for Jesus, then we are people who don’t actually know him. … He’s not calling them to a set of rules. He’s not calling them into a kind of a party that they could get better motion in the society through. He is calling them first to himself.”

KB is careful about who he aims that at. He has spent years in the Christian music industry, touring with CCM and CHH acts, and he says most of the people he’s worked with “really mean what they’re saying.” He’s also wary of the version of himself that came alive being “brutally honest” with people.

“We have not done well with people who have strayed or fallen,” he said. “We often bury our dead instead of restore them. … I don’t want to primarily be the person that is good at pointing out other people’s flaws. I don’t think that that is good for my soul.”

Which is why the warning he cares most about is the one that applies to him.

“I am paid to be spiritual,” KB said. “There’s an assumption that I am as spiritual as my songs make it seem. And then they pay me to come and do that. … And if something public happened where I’m not that guy, they would not pay me anymore. So there’s sort of a connection between my livelihood and my spiritual performance.”

A friend once told him about a pastor who led a large congregation for years while privately confessing to a few trusted people that he didn’t believe in God at all. When someone asked how he kept it up, the pastor’s answer stuck with KB.

“He said, ‘Man, over the years, I just got good at doing God,’” KB said. “And I think that that is a danger that faces those who get paid to speak God good. … In an era of influencers, everyone’s got a platform now. We have run in vain if all we are doing is simply getting engagement, likes and sort of content scores, but we ourselves are far from God.”

He sees the same pressure outside the church, where faith gets pulled into fights it was never meant to referee. And he thinks the algorithm has taught everyone the same lesson.

“What we’ve learned from the algorithm is what sells better than sex is rage,” he said. “The algorithm is not some alien reality that exists outside of us. It is a very dialed-in reading of the desires of the heart of man and women. … If we can all be angry about the same thing and share a common enemy, we almost can unify around that.”

KB calls himself a “black conscious conservative.” He’s “staunchly pro-life,” and he means it “from the womb to the tomb,” something he said caring for aging family members opened his eyes to. Being pro-life, he said, also means valuing “the life of people who do things that make me very angry.”

On immigration, he draws a line between policy, where he thinks Christians can disagree, and principle, where he doesn’t think they can.

“Principally speaking, we are lovers of the foreigner, because the Scripture says that God is a lover of foreigners, including you,” he said. “You are very much so an immigrant in his world, that he has brought close and he has made you a citizen. … There is no viable biblical expression that includes hostility for the well-being of the people who border us.”

His test for all of it comes from Luke 14, where Jesus tells the crowd that anyone who doesn’t hate their own family and even their own life can’t be his disciple.

“Be where you are in the way that God has convicted you. Be all the way there,” KB said. “But at any point of your identity in that place, whether it’s political, racial, national or sports-related, if anything happens in that space where it feels like the movement is starting to go somewhere that Jesus doesn’t like … on those points, you lost my support.”

Under all the outrage, he thinks, is something most commentary misses.

“People are deeply unsettled. People are deeply unsure, deeply uncertain about tomorrow,” he said. “I feel as though there are a lot of Christian leaders that are not picking up on this. And they think that they’re being helpful by adding their voice to whatever everyone else is already saying. … You’re simply an amplification of the echoes that are already out there, but the echoes are scaring us.”

What he wants to offer instead is what he calls “the peace of Christ that surpasses all understanding because it flows from another world,” from “a kingdom that cannot be shaken.”

“Do you realize that empires expire?” he said.

The album’s longest stretch on any one idea is a skit called “No Feeling Lasts Forever,” built for one specific night: the one where someone is fighting temptation alone. KB designed it to be played front to back until the moment passes. He’s watched friends survive nights like that, including people who “struggled with suicide and self-harm.”

“These thoughts lose their strength over trusting God and resisting what the emotion or the thought is asking them to do,” he said. “If you can make it to the morning, if you can get through the night.”

items.title: St. Francis and the Grammar of Gratitude
items.author: Dr. Chad Engelland
items.summary:
Dr. Chad Engelland

There is no being thankful for if there’s no being thankful to. It belongs to the very grammar of the word “thanks.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Chad Engelland

Karl Marx famously described religion as the opiate for the masses, a kind of consolation prize for those whose lives are full of empty harvests, the fruit of their labors continually taken from them by capitalists. With hands empty, they pin all their hope on some heavenly reward. 

But what of those whose hearts are full? Have they then no need of religion?

Of American holidays, surely the best is Thanksgiving, that wonderful time of gathering with family and friends and being grateful for the goods we have together. God has blessed the harvest of our year, and we are grateful, celebrating with delicious food and lively conversation.

In his volume on St. Francis, G. K. Chesterton astutely observes regarding the challenge of those we today call nones, “Rossetti makes the remark somewhere, bitterly but with great truth, that the worst moment for the atheist is when he is really thankful and has nobody to thank.” 

For Chesterton, religion is not the opiate of the masses but the song of the great-souled and grateful.

Is Chesterton too severe with the nones? What, after all, is burdensome about wanting to sing but having no one to sing to? We could say that it belongs to the very logic of the experience of gratitude, that it involves being grateful to someone. As a priest put it in one particularly memorable Thanksgiving homily, there is no being thankful for if there’s no being thankful to. It belongs to the very grammar of the word “thanks.”

We need only think of Dorothy Day for an example of someone whose heart, full of gratitude for the gift of her child, led her to leave behind “none” and talk of religion as “opiate” and instead acknowledge the existence of God the creator, the giver of this gift. 

The experience of fundamental goods as great gifts urges us to want to give thanks, but if the nones have no one to thank, their hearts ache, feeling frustratingly unfulfilled.

It is here that the life of St. Francis takes on such importance eight centuries after his death.

Chesterton reads Francis as a master of giving thanks, someone who lived out this essential spirit by properly fathoming creation as a gift. To this end, Chesterton formulated one of those great Chestertonian lines, the sort of which we would do well to commit to memory and drill daily into our children: “All goods look better when they look like gifts.”

Why might that be? Why might a good look better when it looks like a gift? The answer is seen most transparently when the gift is of little worth. So, for example, the little child takes a flower from her parents’ yard and gifts it to her mother, who receives it with joy. The value of the gift is the intention the child invests with the flower. Giving enhances goods by bathing them in love.

We can take any creature as a good, but to take it as a gift is even better. That’s what Nietzsche misses when he says positing God as the creator drains the world of its goodness. It is not just that God is better than creation: it’s that creation is better than cosmos. 

Think about it. The Greek world rested in itself; there were goods, but they were there not as gifts but instead as givens. In the Christian understanding, those self-same givens are now gifts, which enhances them, for being itself is better when it looks like a gift.

The gift, invested with such an intention, calls for reciprocity; it calls for a response. Not a reciprocal gift that turns the gift into an exchange of presents but the act of acceptance that brings the giving to its proper fulfillment.

It is here again that St. Francis excelled. He shows us the face of the Christian troubadour who sees the world marked with the gratuity of love. At the close of the volume, Chesterton writes,

He was above all things a great giver; and he cared chiefly for the best kind of giving which is called thanksgiving. If another great man wrote a grammar of assent, he may well be said to have written a grammar of acceptance; a grammar of gratitude. He understood down to its very depths the theory of thanks; and its depths are a bottomless abyss. He knew that the praise of God stands on its strongest ground when it stands on nothing. He knew that we can best measure the towering miracle of the mere fact of existence if we realise that but for some strange mercy we should not even exist.

God the creator had mercy on us by snatching us from nothing and loving us into being. The fundamental duty and glory of life is to practice the grammar of gratitude, to see fellow creatures as ontological siblings, to see mother earth as our common sister before God the Father, and to praise the giver of every good and perfect gift.

If every good is better when it is seen as a gift, then Francis—as good as he is—appears even better when we see him as God’s gift to us.

Indeed, even after 800 years, the world still has something to learn from this master of thanksgiving who shows us the faith enhances our perception of the goodness of things.

items.title: It Is Poland’s Moment for Choosing
items.author: Simon Olech
items.summary:
Simon Olech

Poland must decide whether to remain a Catholic nation or submit to the secular West.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Simon Olech

The College Beat: ARTICLE XXII

. . .

Poland must decide whether to remain a Catholic nation or submit to the secular West.

I am often met with happy faces at school whenever I say I am Polish. Students at Franciscan University of Steubenville admire legendary figures like Pope St. John Paul II and St. Maximilian Kolbe—individuals who dedicated their lives to serving God and their fellow man. Their stories are ingrained into the Polish archetype, defining the country’s rich, religious history.

My parents escaped from Communist Poland shortly before the fall of the Iron Curtain, finding freedom and opportunity in the United States of America. Growing up in a Polish household in the Pacific Northwest, I was raised to love my country while simultaneously embracing my European ancestral roots. 

The Catholic faith was a central part of my childhood. I learned about my parents’ homeland and its deep ties to religion, which began more than a thousand years ago when Prince Mieszko I was baptized in an event known as the Baptism of Poland. 

Poland remains a stronghold of Catholicism in Europe, especially when compared to other countries like France, Italy, and Spain, which were once visible hearts of the Church. These nations have become shells of their former spiritual selves, lacking the love and respect for religion that once defined their societies. That is not to say Catholicism is no longer present—Pope Leo XIV’s recent trip to Paris proves it is—but it has faded out of the mainstream and is no longer central to the once religiously rich cultures.

However, this secularism has slowly been spreading into Poland, which is experiencing the same spiritual fatigue other nations have already acceded to. The phenomenon is worrying, especially to a Catholic who admires Poland’s historically deep faith.

On November 7, 2026, a young man killed ten people—three of whom were his family members—and injured fifteen in the Krakow town square, one of the most visited locations in Europe. A mass shooting event like this was thoroughly unprecedented for the country.

School stabbings also rose over the past few months as children have wounded teachers, staff, and fellow classmates with sharp objects, one resulting in the death of a custodian. The Associated Press went so far as to state that “school violence is a new phenomenon” in Poland, suggesting that the country and its younger generations are headed toward a more divisive and hostile society—one antithetical to Christian values. 

Moreover, Poland is adopting secular laws that are fundamentally opposed to Catholic teaching and violate both historical standards and natural law. 

Last March, the Supreme Administrative Court began recognizing so-called same-sex marriages from other European Union states, a decision corrupting the definition of marriage and permitting sinful relationships.

Additionally, as of 2025, it is legal to change one’s gender in Poland. The Polish Supreme Court ruled that transgender youth no longer need to involve their parents in a case to change their officially recognized gender, showing how far it has shifted towards a secular society. These sorts of changes cannot coexist in a Catholic nation because they represent an ideology fundamentally opposed to Church teachings.

Even more troubling is the incessant demand for increased abortion access. Pro-abortion protestors have been wreaking havoc across the country while Poland barely holds onto its strict guardrails, which allow the procedure only if the mother’s life is in danger or she has been raped. As a result, abortion pills have become the go-to method for killing one’s child as new organizations like Abortion Dream Team are formed to facilitate this life-ending poison.

It is important to note that these social changes are occurring during a time of great economic development. Poland recently entered into the world’s top twenty economies as its national income surpassed $1 trillion, revealing the strides it has made since its time under Communist rule. However, it seems like these improvements have led to a decrease in citizens’ desires for religion and a turn towards secular culture—problems impacting both the short- and long-term future of the nation.

Money corrupts men and can corrupt nations when religion and its guiding principles are swapped out for those of greed and pleasure. Of course, that is not to say that these strides in wealth are bad or that Poland has surrendered to them—quite the opposite. Just look at the Polish Independence Day March, where Poles paraded religious images around the city for hours (while a prominent Western media outlet labeled it “far-right,” as if to dissuade such behavior). Poland has pulled itself out of decades of destruction to become an extremely successful nation, and the country should use its blessings to guide its citizens towards virtue. 

With that being said, living with everything one needs makes it easy to abandon prayer, weekly Mass, and the sacraments while pursuing pleasurable activities and crafting a worldly lifestyle. After a while, one may ask: “Why even go to Church?”

Poland cannot remain a Catholic nation while legalizing excessively sinful behavior, embracing those who do not respect nor assimilate to the culture, and breathing the same secular air plaguing much of Western Europe.

Unfortunately, data shows that this is already taking place. Looking at the 2011 census, one will notice that almost 88 percent of the Polish population, numbering 33.7 million people, identified as part of the Roman Catholic Church, a lofty sum compared with other nations. More recently, the 2021 census shows that 27.1 million people, or 71.3 percent of the population, identify as Roman Catholic. Within the span of just ten years, over five million people left the Church.

Simultaneously, the number of people professing no religious belief almost tripled, hitting 6.9 percent in 2021, while the number who refused to answer grew from 7.1 percent to 20.5 percent. Younger Poles are also no longer willing to go to Church at the same rate as their parents and grandparents, as only 23 percent practiced regularly in 2021 compared with 69 percent in 1992. 

This is indicative of a fundamental shift in Poland’s relationship with religion that, if unaddressed and unchanged, will undoubtedly restructure the nation’s identity and relationship with Catholicism. 

Looking back at Poland’s rich and fruitful Christian history, one will quickly find examples of overcoming assaults by hostile powers, often turning to Christ and the Blessed Mother for aid. The difference now is that Poland can no longer concretely identify the enemies confronting its traditions and faith because it is slowly reducing its bond with the Church—its most integral institution. 

Under Communist rule, the Soviet-backed government distributed anti-Catholic propaganda, burned churches, promoted atheism, and harassed clergy to hollow out the Church from within to make space for a Communist, atheist state, completely contrary to the nation’s acknowledged and protected culture. These abuses formed some of the twentieth century’s greatest heroes, such as Jerzy Popiełuszko, a thirty-seven-year-old martyred priest who continued to voice disapproval of the Communist party despite death threats, and Pope John Paul II, who became instrumental in ending the Cold War. 

Today, Poland is experiencing great difficulty recognizing the secularizing effects of their success and is failing to remain steadfast in their traditions and faith. The further entangled they become with the modernist elements of the West, especially those promoting a globalist agenda destined to make every nation homogeneous, the more difficult this will become. 

Poland, the country of my forefathers and the millions of US immigrants who contributed to the improvement of this great nation, is in a moment of choosing. It must decide whether it will continue the legacy left by its ancestors and heroes of the faith, or if it will give in to the forces of secularism and modernization that intend to reduce its love of Christ and nation to that of a secularized West. The choice rests in the hearts and hands of the Polish people.

Niech żyje Polska!
